descriptions.name: Personal & Professional Development
descriptions.displayText: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

descriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability
descriptions.displayText: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

descriptions.name: Econometrics
descriptions.displayText: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. descriptions.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
descriptions.displayText: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. audience.comparisonExplanation: This academic-core comparison covers Groningen’s documented interdisciplinary foundations, research methods, responsible-leadership development, Living Lab and thesis/portfolio requirements. The separate 30-EC minor is identified as choice space; the unverified 65 EC of major/elective study are excluded. The UCR programmes are broader educational responses to this common core. They do not establish a match to an external formal major, equivalent research culmination or a complete Groningen degree pathway.

componentNotes.y2-living-lab: Entry requires completion of all foundation and Skills Lab courses. This 10 EC project brings students, academic supervisors and external partners together to frame a research question, analyse evidence and produce practical recommendations or another agreed output.
componentNotes.y3-minor: The minor semester can include an exchange, an internship or courses from another faculty.
componentNotes.y3-capstone: The final 10 EC capstone combines supervised research (70%) with a personal and social-responsibility portfolio (30%). The portfolio develops across the degree; both parts count within the same 10 EC.
